a: Pointed pen nibs come in hundreds of varieties distinguished by flexibility, sharpness, and tine responsiveness—popular choices include the Leonardt EF Principal (moderate flexibility, very fine hairlines), Nikko G (stiffer, more durable, excellent for beginners), Brause Steno (flexible with good snap-back), and Hunt 101 (very flexible for dramatic shading). New nibs are coated with a protective oil or lacquer that prevents ink from adhering, so they must be cleaned before first use by wiping with rubbing alcohol, passing through a flame briefly, or brushing with toothpaste and rinsing thoroughly. Broad edge nibs include the Speedball C-series (C-0 through C-6, with C-0 producing the widest strokes) for Italic and Gothic scripts, and the Brause Bandzug series for precise, consistent widths in formal hands.

a: Calligraphy inks vary significantly in consistency, drying time, and water resistance: India ink is opaque, permanent, and contains shellac that can clog nibs if not cleaned immediately; sumi ink (Japanese stick ink ground on a suzuri stone or liquid sumi) produces rich, deep black tones with good flow for both pointed and broad edge work; walnut ink crystals (soluble in water) create warm brown tones favored by calligraphers for historical scripts and a vintage look, and they clean up easily without damaging nibs. Paper choice is critical—highly textured or absorbent papers catch nibs and cause ink bleeding, while smooth, hard-surfaced papers like Rhodia (with Clairefontaine vellum), Tomoe River, and Strathmore 400 Series Drawing paper provide the tooth and ink resistance needed for crisp lines. For brush lettering, HP Premium32 Laserjet paper is a budget-friendly favorite that handles heavy ink laydown without bleeding, while Canson XL Marker Paper works well for alcohol-based markers.

a: Brush pens range from water-based (Tombow Dual Brush, Pentel Aquash, Ecoline Brush Pen) that blend easily with water for watercolor effects and allow re-inking, to alcohol-based markers (Copic Sketch, Winsor & Newton Promarker) that produce vibrant, permanent colors ideal for illustration and lettering but require marker-specific paper to prevent bleed-through. Water-based brush pens offer easier cleaning and blending but may fray tips faster, while alcohol markers layer beautifully and dry instantly without reactivating. For beginners, the Tombow Dual Brush is universally recommended for its resilient felt tip, dual-ended design (brush tip and fine bullet tip), and extensive color range, while the Pentel Fude Touch Sign Pen provides a firmer, more controlled brush tip for those transitioning from regular handwriting to brush lettering.

a: A complete pointed pen calligraphy starter kit includes: an oblique pen holder (which positions the nib at the correct writing angle for Copperplate and Spencerian scripts) or a straight pen holder (preferred by many for broad edge and modern calligraphy), a selection of nibs (Nikko G for durability, Leonardt EF Principal for fine hairlines), India or sumi ink, a small ink well with a weighted base to prevent tipping, smooth practice paper (Rhodia dot pads are ideal), and a T-square or rolling ruler for guidelines. The workspace should have good lighting (daylight-balanced lamp recommended), a slightly slanted surface (a drawing board or adjustable table), paper towels or a rag for wiping nibs, a small cup of water for cleaning, and a comfortable chair that allows proper posture to prevent hand fatigue during long practice sessions.
